problem: Gradient-descent planners such as Universal Planning Networks (UPN) need many expert trajectories, use a fixed planning loss and a deterministic dynamics model, and cannot adapt to a shift in perception. This makes them hard to transfer from simulation to a real mobile robot with an onboard camera. Prior sim-to-real work mostly assumes an off-board camera and does not address mobile navigation.
motivation: Training on a real robot is costly and dangerous, while simulation and off-policy real data are cheap. A latent encoding with no physical meaning gives no separate supervision for perception, so standard adversarial sim-to-real transfer (which needs a position-supervised encoder) does not apply directly. The paper asks whether a UPN-style planner can be pre-trained in simulation and transferred with few real demonstrations.
key_idea: Improve UPN with a stochastic dynamics model, an MLP planning loss that is meta-learned through the outer imitation loss, and smoothness and consistency regularizers. Pre-train it in simulation, adversarially align the real-image encoder's latent distribution to the frozen sim encoder using unlabeled images, then fine-tune on a few real demonstrations.
insight: Each planner component (stochasticity, learned MLP loss, regularization) helps: the full Model A converges faster and to a lower outer loss than the ablated variants B-H and vanilla UPN (Fig. 4). Adversarial encoder transfer reduces the number of real expert trajectories needed for a given outer loss by about 5-8x (Table I, e.g. 1250 vs 230 at loss 0.10). The learned MLP loss is high near the lane center and increases away from it, so it learns a sensible task-specific cost (Fig. 6).
method: Stochastic forward dynamics: the latent transition x̂_{t+1} ~ g_θ(x̂_t, â_t, ε) with Gaussian noise ε, for robustness on a real robot.
Meta-learned planning loss: an MLP L_MLP(x̂_g, x_g) replaces the fixed L2/Huber inner-loop loss. Its parameters ζ are updated by the outer imitation loss.

Smoothness and consistency regularization: L_smooth penalizes the distance between successive latent states. L_consist forces g_θ(f_φ(o_t), a_t, ε) to match f_φ(o_{t+1}, ε) at every step. a_t is the expert action with 80% probability, otherwise the current planned action.

Two-loop UPN-style training: the inner loop optimizes the action sequence by gradient descent on L_plan. The outer loop applies an MSE imitation loss against expert actions to update θ, φ and ζ. Training uses curriculum over horizon length and over task (lane following before turning).

Adversarial encoder transfer: freeze the source encoder, initialize the target encoder from it, and train a 3-layer MLP discriminator (ADDA-style) on unlabeled, unpaired sim and real images so real latents match sim latents.
Real fine-tuning: attach the sim-trained dynamics and MLP loss to the target encoder and fine-tune the whole model on a few joystick-collected real expert trajectories.

setting.backbone: UPN-style planner: CNN encoder + fully connected stochastic dynamics model + MLP loss (trained from scratch); 3-layer MLP discriminator
setting.training_data: Simulated joystick expert trajectories in the Duckietown simulator (e.g. 2000 demos for pre-training in Fig. 7), sim and real unlabeled image banks (sim with domain randomization), and a few real expert trajectories for fine-tuning (tens to hundreds)
setting.observation: monocular onboard RGB camera images (current and goal image)
setting.action_space: continuous low-level control actions of the Duckiebot, planned as a sequence over a horizon

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark is used. Results are given in figures (completion rate, reward, loss curves in Figs. 4-8) plus Table I, which reports the number of real trajectories needed for a given outer loss (not SR/SPL).
results: In Duckietown simulation, the full Model A outperforms vanilla UPN and the ablated variants in convergence and in reward and completion rate. On the real robot it achieves more than 50% average completion rate even from a -45° initial angle in the left lane, and it beats a domain randomization baseline (shown in figures). With transfer, the real trajectories needed for the same outer loss drop, e.g. 230 vs 1250 at loss 0.10 and 25 vs 200 at loss 0.35.
limitations: Evaluated only on simple Duckietown tasks (lane following and left turn) with no standard navigation benchmarks or numeric success metrics; the main real-robot results are in figures.
Still needs some real expert demonstrations and unlabeled real images, and adversarial training converges imperfectly.
The baseline comparison is limited to domain randomization and UPN ablations.
builds_on: Zhang et al. adversarial discriminative sim-to-real transfer
compares_to: Ablated variants of the planner (Models B-G)
